idiom_name: AtomicReference CAS loop over a case-class state
implementation_notes: Scala has no STM in its standard library today, and the honest realisation is the same validate-then-act loop as everywhere else, expressed well because of the language's shape: a `case class` state gives you structural equality for free (so conflict detection is one `==` against the observed snapshot) and a `copy` method that produces the next state without mutating anything, which is exactly STM's deferred write set. Put that state behind an `AtomicReference`, read it once, `copy` it, compute, and `compareAndSet`. Scala's real strength here is that immutability is the default idiom, so the precondition STM cares about most - cheap, safe snapshots - is met without effort. Where higher-level concurrency structure is needed, Scala's idiom is Akka-style actors, which achieve mutual exclusion by confinement and are the honest answer for the majority of cases; an STM or a CAS loop is for the residual cases where state must genuinely be shared rather than owned. Scala's match types and sealed traits also make a hand-rolled transaction result (`TransactionResult[T]`) pleasant to express, which matters because the retry decision has to be explicit rather than hidden in an exception.
pitfalls: Using a mutable collection inside the case class, so the snapshot reference silently changes and conflict detection compares the same object to itself.
Copying the state with the same version and then compare_and_set-ing it: publishing an identical snapshot makes the commit meaningless.
Returning an exception for a conflict instead of a value, which forces every caller into a try/catch and makes the retry invisible in the type.
Blocking inside the body (a Future.await), which holds the window open for every conflicting transaction.
Using an actor when state is genuinely shared and large: actor messages copy the state on send, which is worse than an STM snapshot for big structures.
